blocks.content: The Proxy Design Pattern is a structural pattern that acts as a gatekeeper or stand-in for another object, giving you full control over how it is accessed.
Some objects are too costly to create upfront, too sensitive to expose directly, or hidden behind a network. Handing clients direct access to these is rarely a smart move.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245784575-5f103cc0.png
A proxy steps in when you need to:

["Postpone object creation until it is actually required (lazy loading).","Guard sensitive resources behind permission checks or request throttling.","Quietly inject behavior like caching, logging, or retries without touching the original class."]
items: Postpone object creation until it is actually required (lazy loading).
Guard sensitive resources behind permission checks or request throttling.
Quietly inject behavior like caching, logging, or retries without touching the original class.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245784682-2b06ba5a.png

The proxy plants itself right between the client and the real object. Every request passes through it first it then decides whether to forward it, block it, or enrich it with extra logic before reaching the destination.
1. The Problem: Eager Loading
Imagine you are building a simple document viewer. Users open an app and see a list of documents, but only read a few of them.
The naive approach loads every document upfront:
Here is what happens at startup:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245784775-cef94e6b.png
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: Where This Goes Wrong
1. Wasted Memory All documents load at startup even if the user never opens them. Ten documents means ten unnecessary loads.
2. No Extra Behavior Want to log when a document is opened? You have to modify Document directly and mix in extra responsibilities.
3. One Class Doing Too Much Document manages its content and also decides when to load it. These are two different jobs crammed into one class.
What We Actually Need
A better design should:
["Load a document only when the user actually opens it.","Add logging or access checks without modifying Document.","Keep everything working the same way for the rest of the app."]
items: Load a document only when the user actually opens it.
Add logging or access checks without modifying Document.
Keep everything working the same way for the rest of the app.

blocks.content: This is exactly what the Proxy Pattern solves.
2. What is the Proxy Pattern?

The Proxy Pattern is a structural pattern that puts a middle-man in front of a real object to manage how and when it gets reached. The client never directly touches the real object it goes through the proxy, which decides what to do with every incoming request.
Two core ideas define it:

1. Identical Interface The proxy wears the same mask as the real object. Both implement the same interface, so the client cannot tell the difference. It just calls methods and gets results no idea what is actually behind the curtain.

2. Request Interception Every call passes through the proxy first. It can hold back the real object's creation, verify user permissions, serve a cached result, or silently record the activity all without the client suspecting a thing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245784938-d6f4b8a2.png
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

blocks.content: The Four Participants
1. Service BankAccount The common interface shared by both the proxy and the real object. The client only ever interacts with this interface and stays completely unaware of what lies underneath.

2. RealService RealBankAccount The actual object doing the real work. In a banking app, this is the class that connects to the database and processes transactions. It is sensitive and expensive direct access is a bad idea.

3. Proxy BankAccountProxy The gatekeeper. It sits in front of RealBankAccount and only lets requests through after running checks. It can also answer lightweight queries like account number lookups without ever waking up the real object.

4. Client BankingApp The consumer that works purely through the BankAccount interface. It calls methods, gets responses, and has absolutely no knowledge of whether it is speaking to a proxy or the real account object.
Types of Proxies
Depending on the situation, a proxy can play different roles:

["Virtual Proxy: Delays spinning up the real object until the very last moment (lazy creation).","Protection Proxy: Verifies identity or role before granting access to restricted operations.","Remote Proxy: Represents an object that physically lives on a different machine or server.","Caching Proxy: Remembers previous results and skips redundant calls to the real object.","Smart Proxy: Quietly wraps calls with audit logs, usage counters, or performance metrics."]
items: Virtual Proxy: Delays spinning up the real object until the very last moment (lazy creation).
Protection Proxy: Verifies identity or role before granting access to restricted operations.
Remote Proxy: Represents an object that physically lives on a different machine or server.
Caching Proxy: Remembers previous results and skips redundant calls to the real object.
Smart Proxy: Quietly wraps calls with audit logs, usage counters, or performance metrics.

blocks.content: 3. How It Works
Here is the Proxy workflow for our document viewer, step by step:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785093-d5387b1e.png
Step 1: Create the proxy The client creates a DocumentProxy with just the filename. Nothing is read from disk. The proxy is instant and nearly weightless.
Step 2: No loading happens The real RealDocument does not exist yet. Zero disk activity, zero memory used for content.
Step 3: Call a cheap operation The client calls getName(). The proxy returns the stored filename directly without touching the real document at all.
Step 4: Call an expensive operation The client calls open(). The proxy checks if the real document exists it does not so it creates one, which triggers the actual file read.
Step 5: Delegate to the real object With the real document now created, the proxy hands the open() call straight to it.
Step 6: Subsequent calls skip creation The client calls open() again. The proxy sees the real document already exists and delegates immediately with no loading overhead.
4. Implementing the Proxy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785190-8332b1ed.png
1. Create the Proxy Class

TheDocumentProxyimplements the sameDocumentinterface asRealDocument, so the client can use it interchangeably. It stores just the filename and only creates the real document whenopen()is actually called.
2. Client Code
From the client's perspective nothing changes at all. It still works with Document references. But now instead of loading everything upfront, it gets lightweight proxies that only load on demand.

blocks.content: 5. Extending the Design: Other Proxy Types
blocks.text: 5. Extending the Design: Other Proxy Types

blocks.content: One of the most powerful things about the Proxy pattern is how naturally it stretches to cover different problems. The virtual proxy we just built handles lazy loading. But the exact same structure can enforce access rules, record activity, and serve cached results all without touching the real object or rewriting the client.
1. Adding a Protection Proxy
A protection proxy gates access based on who is making the request. For example, only users with a ADMIN role should be allowed to open confidential documents.

The key decision here is where to pass the user context. Changing the open() method signature would break the Document interface. Instead, the role is injected through the proxy's constructor the interface stays clean and the client code stays the same.
The Document interface is completely untouched. An admin gets through every time. A regular user gets blocked the moment the filename contains "confidential".
2. Adding a Logging Proxy

A logging proxy silently wraps every method call and records it for auditing, debugging, or usage tracking. It captures a timestamp before and after each operation so you have a full trail of activity.
Notice the logging proxy wraps anyDocument, not justRealDocument. You can stack it directly on top of the virtual proxy like this:
Document doc = new LoggingDocumentProxy(new DocumentProxy("resume.pdf"));
The logging proxy records the call, then passes it down to the virtual proxy, which handles the lazy loading. Each proxy owns exactly one concern and nothing more.
6. Practical Example: API Request Caching Proxy
blocks.text: 6. Practical Example: API Request Caching Proxy

blocks.content: To show the Proxy pattern in a completely different domain, let's build an API request caching system. The interface defines a simple fetch operation. The real implementation simulates a slow external API call. The caching proxy stores responses and returns saved results for repeated requests.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245785346-10744c8b.png

Response from [/api/users]

--- Same request again (cache hit) ---

--- Different request (cache miss) ---
RealApi: Calling external API: /api/products?status=active
Response from [/api/products?status=active]

--- Clear cache and retry ---
CachingProxy: Cache cleared.
RealApi: Calling external API: /api/users
Response from [/api/users]

blocks.content: The first request takes a full 100 milliseconds hitting the external API. The identical second request comes back instantly from cache. Once the cache is cleared, the same endpoint hits the real API again. The client works through theApiServiceinterface the entire time, completely unaware that caching is happening underneath.
